disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by recurrent, intrusive thoughts, images, or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the person feels driven to perform. These symptoms are time-consuming or cause significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The course is often chronic with waxing and waning severity, frequently exacerbated by stress, increased responsibility, or role transitions. OCD is distinguished from generalized anxiety and other disorders by the presence of specific, stereotyped obsessions and compulsions that are recognized as excessive or unreasonable at some point and are not solely attributable to psychotic processes or the direct effects of substances or medical conditions.

narrative.stressor: Edward’s pattern of being highly structured and meticulous had long been seen as a strength, especially through graduate school and the early years of his mechanical engineering job. During a major product rollout last year, he was put in charge of coordinating multiple design teams, managing tight client deadlines, and ensuring compliance with new sustainability standards, all while studying for the PE exam in his off-hours. Around this period, he began spending increasingly long hours at his desk well after everyone else had left, rechecking design files and project plans in a way that started to interfere with his sleep, jogging routine, and social life with the paddleboarding club. The situation came to a head when he missed a key beach clean‑up event he had organized because he couldn’t pull himself away from repeatedly reviewing a relatively minor CAD change; his manager later gently pointed out that his productivity was paradoxically dropping, which prompted Edward to seek psychiatric help after recognizing that his own mental routines felt out of his control.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep getting stuck redoing the same checks and routines over and over at work, even when I know they’re unnecessary, and it’s starting to derail my projects and my life.”

narrative.stressor: For several years, Waleska’s tendency toward worry was mostly managed through her structured lesson plans, dancing, and nightly journaling. Things shifted when her parents’ health began to decline and she took on more responsibility, regularly driving to help them with appointments while trying to maintain her teaching job and community activities in Willis. As family expectations intensified—especially around being the dependable daughter who kept everything organized—she found herself increasingly preoccupied outside of school with whether she had forgotten something important for her students or her parents, which made it harder to enjoy salsa nights or even relax at home. After she started arriving early and staying late at school because she felt unable to leave until she had mentally reviewed and rewritten plans in her head multiple times, her principal noticed her exhaustion and suggested she talk to a professional; Waleska agreed after realizing her worry-driven routines around planning were taking over evenings she once spent with family and church friends.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind keeps getting stuck on the same worrying thoughts about what I might have forgotten or done wrong, and I can’t seem to shut them off even when I’m not at school.”

narrative.stressor: Hector had always been a meticulous planner, using spreadsheets to manage projects, travel, and even his vinyl collection, but he generally balanced this with salsa dancing, community events, and pickup basketball. When his company underwent a major reorganization two years ago, he was promoted to oversee a larger IT infrastructure portfolio, including cybersecurity for several high-profile clients, which dramatically increased his sense of responsibility and the potential consequences of mistakes. Over the following months, he started staying later and later at the office and at home, repeatedly reviewing configurations and incident reports, and turning down salsa socials and tech meetups he used to enjoy because he felt compelled to keep checking and rechecking his work. The tipping point came when he missed a critical family celebration and then had a minor panic episode on the train home after realizing that, despite all his late nights, he still felt unable to trust that things were "safe"; a colleague who noticed his deteriorating sleep and performance urged him to see a psychiatrist, and Hector finally agreed when he recognized that his checking routines had become unmanageable and were crowding out nearly everything else in his life.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m stuck in this loop of double- and triple-checking my work for hours, and I can’t move on even when I know it’s already done right.”
